IntroHero.headline.message: A whole 64-bit ARM computer in a browser tab
IntroHero.headline.note: The introduction's headline (the page's first words for a new visitor). A title: no period.

IntroHero.lede.message: $t(common:product.name) emulates the hardware, not the operating system. Linux can't tell the difference, so the Debian, Arch, and Alpine images made for a Raspberry Pi or an ARM cloud server boot here as they are, with their own kernels.
IntroHero.lede.note: The introduction's first paragraph, under the headline: what the emulator is and what follows from it. This page names distributions and products, unlike the rest of the web app's words.

IntroHero.speed.message: The guest's code is compiled to WebAssembly while it runs. That is fast enough for a desktop with Firefox in it, video and 3D included. Nothing is installed, and the machine runs on your computer, not on a server.
IntroHero.speed.note: The introduction's second paragraph: how it is fast, what that allows, and that it runs locally.

IntroFacts.title.note: Title of the introduction's second section. No period.

IntroFacts.lede.message: The machine is whole, so the software doesn't have to be adapted to it. Whatever ships for 64-bit ARM Linux is a candidate, closed-source programs included.
IntroFacts.lede.note: Paragraph under the title of the introduction's “What runs on it” section.

IntroFacts.cores.note: A figure in a readout of the introduction's “What runs on it” section, in large digits. What it counts is IntroFacts.cores.counts.

IntroFacts.cores.counts.note: What the figure “8” counts, under its readout on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroFacts.cores.words.message: Each core runs on a thread of its own, and the guest's atomic instructions are real atomic operations.
IntroFacts.cores.words.note: The sentence under the readout “8 cores” on the introduction: what stands behind the figure.

IntroFacts.ram.note: A figure in a readout of the introduction's “What runs on it” section, in large digits. What it counts is IntroFacts.ram.counts.

IntroFacts.ram.counts.note: What the figure “16 GiB” counts, under its readout on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroFacts.ram.words.message: WebAssembly gives a program 4 GiB at most. Past the first 3 GiB, the guest's memory is spread over more memories and shown to Linux as NUMA nodes.
IntroFacts.ram.words.note: The sentence under the readout “16 GiB of memory” on the introduction: what stands behind the figure.

IntroFacts.tests.note: A figure in a readout of the introduction's “What runs on it” section, in large digits. What it counts is IntroFacts.tests.counts.

IntroFacts.tests.counts.note: What the figure “61,425” counts, under its readout on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroFacts.tests.words.message: These are dEQP's lists for OpenGL ES 2 and 3, the tests Android requires a GPU driver to pass, run on Chromium's software renderer. On a real GPU, a few fail where that GPU's own driver does.
IntroFacts.tests.words.note: The sentence under the readout “61,425 graphics tests passed, none failed” on the introduction: what stands behind the figure.

IntroFacts.drivers.note: A figure in a readout of the introduction's “What runs on it” section, in large digits. What it counts is IntroFacts.drivers.counts.

IntroFacts.drivers.counts.message: drivers to install in the guest
IntroFacts.drivers.counts.note: What the figure “0” counts, under its readout on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroFacts.drivers.words.message: There is no patched kernel either. The devices are virtio, xHCI, PL011, and GICv3, which Linux has supported for years.
IntroFacts.drivers.words.note: The sentence under the readout “0 drivers to install in the guest” on the introduction: what stands behind the figure.

IntroFacts.desktop.message: A desktop with a browser in it
IntroFacts.desktop.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “What runs on it” section. No period.

IntroFacts.desktop.words.message: Firefox and Chromium run inside the tab, WebGL included. Video is decoded by your GPU through VA-API, so YouTube plays in the guest's browser.
IntroFacts.desktop.words.note: Paragraph of the topic “A desktop with a browser in it” in the introduction's “What runs on it” section.

IntroFacts.vulkan.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “What runs on it” section. No period.

IntroFacts.vulkan.words.message: Vulkan programs run through Mesa's Venus driver onto WebGPU. vkcube, vkmark, and vkQuake work today. It is the newest part and still growing.
IntroFacts.vulkan.words.note: Paragraph of the topic “Vulkan” in the introduction's “What runs on it” section.

IntroFacts.devices.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “What runs on it” section. No period.

IntroFacts.devices.words.message: Plug in a USB device and hand it to the guest. Game controllers, the microphone, and the clipboard reach it too.
IntroFacts.devices.words.note: Paragraph of the topic “Your devices” in the introduction's “What runs on it” section.

IntroFacts.disks.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “What runs on it” section. No period.

IntroFacts.disks.words.message: Open a qcow2 or raw image as its publisher made it, keep it in this browser, and share a folder from your computer. Export the whole disk later, or only what changed.
IntroFacts.disks.words.note: Paragraph of the topic “Your disks and files” in the introduction's “What runs on it” section.

IntroFacts.snapshots.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “What runs on it” section. No period.

IntroFacts.snapshots.words.message: Freeze a running machine, 3D programs and all, and continue later. A snapshot can be saved to a file and opened in another browser.
IntroFacts.snapshots.words.note: Paragraph of the topic “Snapshots” in the introduction's “What runs on it” section.

IntroFacts.networks.words.message: Join your Tailscale network, go online through your own computer, or connect two browsers directly, peer to peer. A machine can have four adapters.
IntroFacts.networks.words.note: Paragraph of the topic “Networks” in the introduction's “What runs on it” section.

IntroCompare.leads.first.words.message: unkernel's demo answers a command 1.3 seconds after you open it, having downloaded 6.7 MiB. Our smallest demo needs about 4 seconds and 25 MB, and our desktop about half a minute.

IntroCompare.leads.browsers.words.message: unkernel runs in Firefox, in Safari, and on iPhones. v86 and JSLinux run nearly anywhere. $t(common:product.name) supports Chromium-based browsers only.

IntroCompare.leads.memory.words.message: unkernel's whole guest fits in 48 MiB, because its kernel isn't emulated. An emulated machine with a stock kernel can't be that small.
IntroCompare.leads.memory.words.note: Paragraph of the entry “Memory” under “Where they lead” on the introduction. The figures are docs/comparison.md §3's.

IntroCompare.leads.syscalls.note: Title of an entry under “Where they lead” on the introduction. No period.

IntroCompare.leads.syscalls.words.message: unkernel's kernel is WebAssembly itself, so a system call is a function call. Here it is an exception the emulated processor takes, as on real hardware, and that costs more.
IntroCompare.leads.syscalls.words.note: Paragraph of the entry “System calls” under “Where they lead” on the introduction. The figures are docs/comparison.md §3's.

IntroTranslate.blocks.note: Screen reader's name for the buttons that choose which captured code the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive) shows.

IntroTranslate.sum.note: Button in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive): shows the captured code of this small C function. A name: no period.

IntroTranslate.sum.look.message: A load in a loop. The WebAssembly looks the address up in the TLB inline and reads the byte itself. The folded slow path is taken only when the page isn't in the TLB. The branch at the end compares the numbers directly, and the flags are only stored for whoever reads them later.
IntroTranslate.sum.look.note: Paragraph beside the C source in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive), for “Summing bytes”: what to notice in this code's translation.

IntroTranslate.move.note: Button in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive): shows the captured code of this small C function. A name: no period.

IntroTranslate.move.look.message: Two pair loads and a pair store through one pointer. The JIT checks the TLB once for the whole group, so the accesses after the first are plain WebAssembly loads and stores, and the group shares one slow path.
IntroTranslate.move.look.note: Paragraph beside the C source in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive), for “Moving a point”: what to notice in this code's translation.

IntroTranslate.collatz.note: Button in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive): shows the captured code of this small C function. A name: no period.

IntroTranslate.collatz.look.message: No memory at all: arithmetic, a conditional select, and a branch. The guest's registers live in WebAssembly locals, which V8 keeps in your processor's registers. The compare writes no flags. The branch after it compares the numbers itself.
IntroTranslate.collatz.look.note: Paragraph beside the C source in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive), for “Collatz steps”: what to notice in this code's translation.

IntroTranslate.total.note: Button in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive): shows the captured code of this small C function. A name: no period.

IntroTranslate.total.look.message: Floating-point code. The addition is one WebAssembly f64.add. The lines around it check that your processor's answer is the one an ARM processor would give: the rounding mode is the default, and no operand or result is a NaN, an infinity, or a denormal. Otherwise the slow path computes it in software.
IntroTranslate.total.look.note: Paragraph beside the C source in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive), for “Adding floats”: what to notice in this code's translation.

IntroTranslate.cap.message: A loop with a branch inside
IntroTranslate.cap.note: Button in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive): shows the captured code of this small C function. A name: no period.

IntroTranslate.cap.look.message: Three blocks of the guest compiled as one WebAssembly function with a loop in it. Each block ran in the interpreter first, was then compiled alone, and joined this function once the loop had run a thousand times.
IntroTranslate.cap.look.note: Paragraph beside the C source in the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive), for “A loop with a branch inside”: what to notice in this code's translation.

IntroTranslate.honest.message: Nothing here is drawn by hand. The guest's code ran in $t(common:product.name), and these are its micro-ops and the WebAssembly it emitted, printed by wasm-tools. The machine code is what {{compiler}} made of that function. V8 says which line a load, a store, or a call came from, so only those light up in the last pane.
IntroTranslate.honest.note: Fine print under the panes of the introduction's code viewer (the CPU's deep dive): where the code shown comes from. {{compiler}} names the V8 version and compiler tier.

IntroHow.cpu.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “How it works” section. No period.

IntroHow.cpu.words.message: An emulator is as fast as the way it runs the guest's code. $t(common:product.name) interprets code that runs a few times and compiles the rest to WebAssembly. On an Apple M4, that reaches about 80% of QEMU's speed at CoreMark, from inside a browser.
IntroHow.cpu.words.note: Paragraph under the topic title “The processor” in the introduction's “How it works” section.

IntroHow.cpu.path.note: Screen reader's name for the row of stages under that topic.

IntroHow.cpu.1.note: Label of stage 1 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.1.line.note: The line under the label of stage 1 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.1.words.message: The guest's code is handled a block at a time: the instructions up to the next branch, 32 at most.
IntroHow.cpu.1.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “The processor” picture on the introduction while stage 1 (“Guest”) is the active one.

IntroHow.cpu.2.note: Label of stage 2 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.2.line.note: The line under the label of stage 2 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.2.words.message: The first time a block runs, it is decoded into micro-ops of 8 bytes, one for each instruction. An interpreter loop runs those. Code that runs only a few times never costs a compilation.
IntroHow.cpu.2.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “The processor” picture on the introduction while stage 2 (“Interpreter”) is the active one.

IntroHow.cpu.3.note: Label of stage 3 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.3.line.note: The line under the label of stage 3 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.3.words.message: Every run is counted. A block that has run 1,000 times is worth compiling, and joins the next batch.
IntroHow.cpu.3.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “The processor” picture on the introduction while stage 3 (“Counter”) is the active one.

IntroHow.cpu.4.note: Label of stage 4 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.4.line.note: The line under the label of stage 4 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.4.words.message: The JIT emits WebAssembly for the block and its neighbors, up to 16 blocks in one function, so a loop stays inside it. The guest's registers become local variables.
IntroHow.cpu.4.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “The processor” picture on the introduction while stage 4 (“JIT”) is the active one.

IntroHow.cpu.5.note: Label of stage 5 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.5.line.note: The line under the label of stage 5 of the “The processor” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.cpu.5.words.message: The browser compiles that WebAssembly to machine code, as it does for any web page. With several cores, all of them share the same compiled code.
IntroHow.cpu.5.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “The processor” picture on the introduction while stage 5 (“V8”) is the active one.

IntroHow.memory.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “How it works” section. No period.

IntroHow.memory.words.message: WebAssembly gives a program 4 GiB of address space, and the emulator needs part of that for itself. The guest can still have 16 GiB, and nearly every access to it is a single load or store.
IntroHow.memory.words.note: Paragraph under the topic title “Memory” in the introduction's “How it works” section.

IntroHow.memory.path.note: Screen reader's name for the row of stages under that topic.

IntroHow.memory.1.note: Label of stage 1 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.memory.1.line.note: The line under the label of stage 1 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.memory.1.words.message: A load or a store in the guest names a virtual address, as on real hardware. The guest's page tables decide what it means.
IntroHow.memory.1.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Memory” picture on the introduction while stage 1 (“Address”) is the active one.

IntroHow.memory.2.note: Label of stage 2 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.memory.2.line.note: The line under the label of stage 2 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.memory.2.words.message: Compiled code looks the page up in a table of recent translations: a shift, a mask, and one compare. On a hit, it adds an offset and has the real address.
IntroHow.memory.2.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Memory” picture on the introduction while stage 2 (“TLB”) is the active one.

IntroHow.memory.3.note: Label of stage 3 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.memory.3.line.note: The line under the label of stage 3 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.memory.3.words.message: Most accesses end here, as a plain WebAssembly load or store. Memory 0 is shared by all cores, and it also holds the emulator's own state.
IntroHow.memory.3.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Memory” picture on the introduction while stage 3 (“Memory 0”) is the active one.

IntroHow.memory.4.note: Label of stage 4 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.memory.4.line.note: The line under the label of stage 4 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.memory.4.words.message: RAM past 3 GiB lives in more WebAssembly memories. Linux is told that each is a NUMA node without processors, so it fills them last.
IntroHow.memory.4.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Memory” picture on the introduction while stage 4 (“More memories”) is the active one.

IntroHow.memory.5.note: Label of stage 5 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.memory.5.line.note: The line under the label of stage 5 of the “Memory” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.memory.5.words.message: When the table has no answer, the instruction runs again in the interpreter. It walks the guest's page tables as a processor would, raises the fault if there is one, and fills the table for next time.
IntroHow.memory.5.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Memory” picture on the introduction while stage 5 (“Miss”) is the active one.

IntroHow.gl.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “How it works” section. No period.

IntroHow.gl.words.message: Nothing in the guest is special. Mesa's driver for virtual machines sends its commands out, and a renderer we wrote plays them on WebGL2.
IntroHow.gl.words.note: Paragraph under the topic title “OpenGL” in the introduction's “How it works” section.

IntroHow.gl.path.note: Screen reader's name for the row of stages under that topic.

IntroHow.gl.1.note: Label of stage 1 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.gl.1.line.note: The line under the label of stage 1 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.gl.1.words.message: A program in the guest calls OpenGL or OpenGL ES, as on any Linux desktop.
IntroHow.gl.1.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction while stage 1 (“Program”) is the active one.

IntroHow.gl.2.note: Label of stage 2 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.gl.2.line.note: The line under the label of stage 2 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.gl.2.words.message: Mesa's virgl driver turns the calls into a stream of commands. It compiles shaders to an intermediate form called TGSI.
IntroHow.gl.2.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction while stage 2 (“Mesa”) is the active one.

IntroHow.gl.3.note: Label of stage 3 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.gl.3.line.note: The line under the label of stage 3 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.gl.3.words.message: The stream leaves through a virtio-gpu device. Textures and buffers aren't copied out: the renderer's thread reads them in the guest's memory, which is shared.
IntroHow.gl.3.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction while stage 3 (“virtio-gpu”) is the active one.

IntroHow.gl.4.note: Label of stage 4 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.gl.4.line.note: The line under the label of stage 4 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.gl.4.words.message: Our renderer decodes the stream in a worker and translates each shader from TGSI to GLSL ES. It also does what WebGL2 can't do by itself, such as BGRA formats, base-vertex draws, and stencil per face.
IntroHow.gl.4.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction while stage 4 (“Renderer”) is the active one.

IntroHow.gl.5.note: Label of stage 5 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.gl.5.line.note: The line under the label of stage 5 of the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.gl.5.words.message: Everything is drawn on one WebGL2 context, once per frame of your display. A frame of the sway desktop costs the guest 6.6 ms this way, against 81 ms when it renders in software.
IntroHow.gl.5.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “OpenGL” picture on the introduction while stage 5 (“WebGL2”) is the active one.

IntroHow.video.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “How it works” section. No period.

IntroHow.video.words.message: A guest that decodes video in software would spend most of its time on it. Here the guest hands the compressed stream over, and your browser's decoder does the work.
IntroHow.video.words.note: Paragraph under the topic title “Video” in the introduction's “How it works” section.

IntroHow.video.path.note: Screen reader's name for the row of stages under that topic.

IntroHow.video.1.note: Label of stage 1 of the “Video” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.video.1.line.note: The line under the label of stage 1 of the “Video” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.video.1.words.message: Firefox, mpv, or GStreamer in the guest asks VA-API to decode a video, as on a PC with a hardware decoder.
IntroHow.video.1.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Video” picture on the introduction while stage 1 (“Player”) is the active one.

IntroHow.video.2.note: Label of stage 2 of the “Video” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.video.2.line.note: The line under the label of stage 2 of the “Video” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.video.2.words.message: Mesa's driver sends each picture's compressed data and its parameters through the same virtio-gpu device as 3D.
IntroHow.video.2.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Video” picture on the introduction while stage 2 (“Mesa”) is the active one.

IntroHow.video.3.note: Label of stage 3 of the “Video” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.video.3.line.note: The line under the label of stage 3 of the “Video” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.video.3.words.message: VA-API hands over slices and parameters, and a browser wants a stream. So the stream is put together again: H.264 with its parameter sets, AV1 with its headers, VP9 as sent.
IntroHow.video.3.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Video” picture on the introduction while stage 3 (“Bitstream”) is the active one.

IntroHow.video.4.note: Label of stage 4 of the “Video” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.video.4.line.note: The line under the label of stage 4 of the “Video” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.video.4.words.message: The browser's VideoDecoder decodes it, on your GPU where it can. H.264, VP9, and AV1 are offered to the guest when your browser has them.
IntroHow.video.4.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Video” picture on the introduction while stage 4 (“WebCodecs”) is the active one.

IntroHow.video.5.note: Label of stage 5 of the “Video” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.video.5.line.note: The line under the label of stage 5 of the “Video” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.video.5.words.message: The decoded picture is written into textures the guest already holds. It never passes through the guest's memory, and the guest's compositor draws it like any other surface.
IntroHow.video.5.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Video” picture on the introduction while stage 5 (“Texture”) is the active one.

IntroHow.vulkan.note: Title of a topic in the introduction's “How it works” section. No period.

IntroHow.vulkan.words.message: This is the deepest stack of the five. Vulkan is close to the hardware, WebGPU is not, and a real Mesa driver sits between them, compiled to WebAssembly.
IntroHow.vulkan.words.note: Paragraph under the topic title “Vulkan” in the introduction's “How it works” section.

IntroHow.vulkan.path.note: Screen reader's name for the row of stages under that topic.

IntroHow.vulkan.1.note: Label of stage 1 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.1.line.note: The line under the label of stage 1 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.1.words.message: A program in the guest calls Vulkan: vkcube, vkQuake, the Godot editor, or a browser's own renderer.
IntroHow.vulkan.1.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction while stage 1 (“Program”) is the active one.

IntroHow.vulkan.2.note: Label of stage 2 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.2.line.note: The line under the label of stage 2 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.2.words.message: Mesa's Venus driver writes the Vulkan commands, nearly as they are, into rings in shared memory. No call has to stop the guest.
IntroHow.vulkan.2.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction while stage 2 (“Mesa”) is the active one.

IntroHow.vulkan.3.note: Label of stage 3 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.3.line.note: The line under the label of stage 3 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.3.words.message: On our side, virglrenderer's own Venus decoder reads the rings. It is the same C code that runs under QEMU, compiled to WebAssembly.
IntroHow.vulkan.3.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction while stage 3 (“Decoder”) is the active one.

IntroHow.vulkan.4.note: Label of stage 4 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.4.line.note: The line under the label of stage 4 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.4.words.message: The decoder calls a Vulkan driver we wrote on Mesa's runtime, whose hardware is WebGPU. Shaders go from SPIR-V through Mesa's NIR to WGSL, with a compiler of ours. What WebGPU lacks is emulated, such as transform feedback, multiview, and logic operations.
IntroHow.vulkan.4.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction while stage 4 (“Driver”) is the active one.

IntroHow.vulkan.5.note: Label of stage 5 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction (drawn in small capitals). A name: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.5.line.note: The line under the label of stage 5 of the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroHow.vulkan.5.words.message: WebGPU draws the frame. It costs 1.0 to 1.8 times what native Vulkan does on an Apple M4, and 1.9 to 3.6 times on an RTX 3070.
IntroHow.vulkan.5.words.note: Paragraph shown under the “Vulkan” picture on the introduction while stage 5 (“WebGPU”) is the active one.

IntroRam.slider.note: Tooltip of the slider in the introduction's memory deep dive: how much RAM the guest gets.

IntroRam.value.note: The slider's value in the introduction's memory deep dive: the RAM chosen.

IntroRam.memory0.message: Memory 0 holds {{size, bytes}} of RAM (NUMA node 0) and the emulator's own 1 GiB
IntroRam.memory0.note: Over the first bar of the introduction's memory deep dive. {{size}} is the guest RAM in WebAssembly memory 0. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroRam.spill.message: Memory {{n}} holds {{size, bytes}} of RAM (NUMA node {{n}})
IntroRam.spill.note: Over a later bar of the introduction's memory deep dive. {{n}} is the WebAssembly memory's number, which is also the NUMA node's; {{size}} its guest RAM. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroRam.legend.node0.message: RAM that compiled code reaches directly
IntroRam.legend.node0.note: Legend of the bars in the introduction's memory deep dive: the guest RAM in memory 0. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroRam.legend.spill.note: Legend of the bars in the introduction's memory deep dive: guest RAM in a later WebAssembly memory. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroRam.legend.own.message: The emulator's own state and heap
IntroRam.legend.own.note: Legend of the bars in the introduction's memory deep dive: the part of memory 0 the emulator keeps for itself. Not a sentence: no period.

IntroRam.words.message: Each bar is one WebAssembly memory, 4 GiB long. Memory 0 can hold 3 GiB less 1 MiB of RAM, because the emulator keeps a gigabyte of it for decoded code and its own data. Whatever is left over goes to more memories, which Linux sees as NUMA nodes and fills last.
IntroRam.words.note: First paragraph under the bars of the introduction's memory deep dive.

IntroRam.cost.message: The other choices were measured and lost. A 64-bit WebAssembly memory cost 6% to 20% of the speed on an x86 PC, and about as much on an Apple M4. Keeping all of RAM in a second memory cost 12% to 40%. With this split, compiled code that works on node 1 takes 1.0 to 1.6 times as long as on node 0, and most machines never get there.
IntroRam.cost.note: Second paragraph under the bars of the introduction's memory deep dive: why RAM is split this way. The figures are docs/architecture.md's and docs/spill-memories.md's.

IntroGuest.label.message: A small machine running in this tab
IntroGuest.label.note: Screen reader's name for the frame beside the introduction's first paragraphs: a small Linux machine that boots by itself when the page opens, with its screen and its serial terminal.

IntroGuest.terminal.note: Screen reader's name for the terminal under the small machine's screen on the introduction.

IntroGuest.start.note: Button over the small machine's empty screen on the introduction, for a visitor whose system asks for less motion: nothing moves until they press it.

IntroGuest.again.note: Button over the small machine's screen on the introduction after the machine powered itself off (the visitor typed poweroff): boots it again.

IntroGuest.caption.waiting.message: A small ARM machine can run here. It boots in about half a second.
IntroGuest.caption.waiting.note: Line under the small machine's empty screen on the introduction before it is started (a visitor who asked for less motion). The time is the measured one: keep it approximate.

IntroGuest.caption.scope.message: This picture is being drawn now, by a machine that started when this page opened.
IntroGuest.caption.scope.note: Line under the small machine's screen on the introduction while its first picture runs alone (an oscilloscope-like figure), before anything shows that it is Linux.

IntroGuest.caption.reveal.message: The machine is an emulated ARM computer running Linux. The picture is a small C program on it, and these are its commands.
IntroGuest.caption.reveal.note: Line under the small machine's screen on the introduction when its terminal starts typing commands (uname, ls): the reveal that the picture comes from a Linux machine.

IntroGuest.caption.ridges.message: A second program. Every instruction it runs is ARM code that $t(common:product.name) compiled to WebAssembly a moment ago.
IntroGuest.caption.ridges.note: Line under the small machine's screen on the introduction while its second picture runs (a flight over a landscape of lines).

IntroGuest.caption.life.message: A third. The whole machine, kernel and programs, came with this page in one file of under 2 MB.
IntroGuest.caption.life.note: Line under the small machine's screen on the introduction while its third picture runs (Conway's Game of Life). The size is the guest image's as downloaded (1.7 MB): keep “under 2 MB”.

IntroGuest.caption.shell.message: The shell is yours. Click the terminal and type top, scope, or cat /toys/life.c.
IntroGuest.caption.shell.note: Line under the small machine's screen on the introduction once its tour is over and its shell waits for the visitor. The three commands are real ones in the guest: don't translate them.

IntroGuest.caption.off.note: Line under the small machine's screen on the introduction after the visitor typed poweroff in its shell.

IntroGuest.counters.message: {{steps}} instructions run, in {{blocks}} blocks compiled to WebAssembly
IntroGuest.counters.note: Small line under the small machine's terminal on the introduction, updated every second: {{steps}} is the count of ARM instructions the machine has executed so far and {{blocks}} the count of code blocks the JIT compiled, both formatted numbers like 1,234,567.
